notice: RN bank batch 130: Mental health case studies: panic disorder, OCD, PTSD and opioid use disorder. Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md. Also carries the bank-wide catalog (catalog.py): the RN Question Bank and every curated test set.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support panic disorder rather than a medical cause.

rationale.correct: Recurrent sudden attacks with avoidance and normal tests suggest panic disorder.

perOption.r2: Behavior change from fear of attacks.
perOption.r5: A trigger that must be addressed, not a support for the diagnosis.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each finding during the attack, indicate its cause.

rows.text: Tingling around the mouth and fingers
Pounding heart
Light-headedness
Shaking and sweating
Muscle cramps in the hands

rationale.correct: Overbreathing and adrenaline explain the symptoms.
references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: During an attack, the nurse's priority is to {{b1}}, using {{b2}}.

options.text: stay with the client and reduce the anxiety
teach coping skills in detail
leave the client alone to calm down
explain the physiology of panic
short, calm sentences and slow breathing together
a paper bag held over the face
a loud, firm voice
long explanations

rationale.correct: Stay, speak simply and guide breathing.

perOption.b1:d: Cannot be processed during an attack.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care during a panic attack.

questions.stem: For each medicine, indicate its role in panic disorder.

rows.text: Sertraline
Lorazepam
Buspirone
Cognitive behavioral therapy (not a medicine)
Venlafaxine

rationale.correct: SSRIs or SNRIs with CBT long term; benzodiazepines only short term.

perOption.r2:c1: Fast relief; dependence with long use.
perOption.r2:c2: Fast relief; dependence with long use.
perOption.r2:c3: Fast relief; dependence with long use.
perOption.r3:c1: Slow; for generalized anxiety, not panic.
perOption.r3:c2: Slow; for generalized anxiety, not panic.
perOption.r3:c3: Slow; for generalized anxiety, not panic.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Generate the panic disorder treatment plan.

exhibits.title: Plan
exhibits.body: Sertraline 25 mg daily, increase slowly. Lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed for 2 weeks. CBT referral.

questions.stem: Which teaching should the nurse give about the new medicines? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sertraline may take 4 to 6 weeks to work
Anxiety may briefly worsen at the start of sertraline
Do not drink alcohol with lorazepam
Do not stop lorazepam suddenly after regular use
Take extra lorazepam before driving to prevent attacks
Stop sertraline once you feel better after a week

rationale.correct: Delayed SSRI effect, avoiding alcohol and not stopping suddenly.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

exhibits.title: Clinic
exhibits.body: Client asks how fast the medicines work.

questions.stem: At 3 months, for each statement or finding, indicate whether it shows progress or needs follow-up.

rows.text: One mild attack this month (was several a week)
"I drove to the supermarket with my CBT homework plan."
"I cut down to one coffee a day."
"I take lorazepam every day now, sometimes three tablets."
"I use slow breathing when I feel it starting."

rationale.correct: Fewer attacks and less avoidance; daily benzodiazepine use needs review.
references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each item, indicate whether it is an obsession or a compulsion.

rows.text: Intrusive fear of contaminating the baby
Washing hands for 30 minutes
Checking the stove 30 times
Unwanted image of the house burning
Counting silently to 50 to cancel a thought

rationale.correct: Obsessions are thoughts; compulsions are acts that relieve anxiety.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: On admission, the nurse should {{b1}}, because stopping rituals suddenly {{b2}}.

options.text: allow time for rituals while setting gradual limits
forbid all handwashing at once
ignore the rituals
point out that the fears are silly
causes severe anxiety
cures OCD quickly
has no effect
reduces depression

rationale.correct: Gradual limits rather than sudden prohibition.

questions.stem: Which parts of the plan should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Exposure and response prevention with the therapist
A schedule that builds in time for meals and rituals
Emollient and gentle skin care for the hands
A high-dose SSRI as prescribed
Reassure the client every time they ask if their hands are clean
Use alcohol hand rub instead of washing

rationale.correct: ERP, a structured schedule, skin care and an SSRI; avoid reassurance cycles.

perOption.f: Worsens cracked skin and is still a ritual.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: The client repeatedly asks, "Are you sure my hands are clean? Are you sure?" Which responses are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: "We agreed to sit with the doubt for 10 minutes, together."
"It sounds really uncomfortable not to be sure."
"Yes, they are definitely clean, I watched you wash them and I promise."
"Please stop asking me that, it is the tenth time this hour."
"Go and wash them again so you feel better."

rationale.correct: Validate and support the agreed plan without reassuring.

content.template: The nurse's first priority is {{b1}}, including {{b2}}.

options.text: a full suicide risk assessment
starting trauma therapy today
teaching sleep hygiene
couples counseling
lethal means counseling about the firearm
advice to keep the gun closer for safety
telling the veteran to drink less only

perOption.b2:a: Storing it away from home reduces risk.

questions.stem: Which parts of the plan should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Trauma-focused therapy such as prolonged exposure or cognitive processing
Sertraline or paroxetine
Prazosin at bedtime for nightmares as prescribed
Treatment for alcohol use
Long-term daily benzodiazepines for sleep
Ask the veteran to describe the trauma in detail at every visit

rationale.correct: Trauma therapy, SSRIs, prazosin and alcohol treatment.

perOption.e: Worsen PTSD outcomes and interact with alcohol.

options.text: Take the first dose at bedtime
Rise slowly from bed at night
Avoid alcohol, which worsens dizziness
Stop the medicine if nightmares improve after one night
Double the dose if a nightmare occurs

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it is accurate or inaccurate about naloxone.

rows.text: Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes, shorter than many opioids
It can cause sudden withdrawal in dependent clients
It has no effect if no opioids are present
One dose always reverses fentanyl permanently
The goal is to restore breathing, not full alertness

rationale.correct: Naloxone is short-acting and titrated to breathing.

perOption.r4:c1: Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
perOption.r4:c2: Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

options.text: open the airway and give rescue breaths with a bag-valve mask
start a naloxone infusion before ventilating
let the client sleep it off
draw a urine drug screen
give naloxone in small IV doses and consider an infusion
discharge home
give flumazenil
give a sedative

rationale.correct: Airway and breathing first, then titrated naloxone.

questions.stem: The next day the client says, "I want to stop using." Which parts of the plan should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offer buprenorphine starting in the hospital
Give a naloxone kit and teach the family to use it
Link to an outpatient program before discharge
Screen for hepatitis C and HIV
Require 30 days of abstinence before medication
Advise detoxification without medication as the best choice

rationale.correct: Buprenorphine, naloxone, linkage and infection screening.

perOption.a: Medication for opioid use disorder lowers death.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate the opioid use disorder plan.

exhibits.title: Next day
exhibits.body: Last fentanyl use 18 hours ago. COWS score pending.

questions.stem: Before the first buprenorphine dose, review the findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the buprenorphine and notify the provider
Explain that starting too early can cause sudden withdrawal
Reassess the COWS score in a few hours
Give the full dose now because the client asked for it
Give naloxone to speed up withdrawal

rationale.correct: Buprenorphine starts when withdrawal is moderate; too early causes precipitated withdrawal.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: At 1 month, for each statement or finding, indicate whether it shows progress or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Taking buprenorphine daily; urine negative for fentanyl
"My sister carries naloxone now."
"I'm also taking my friend's alprazolam to sleep."
Attending a peer support group weekly
"I'll stop buprenorphine next week now that I'm better."

rationale.correct: Recovery under way; benzodiazepine use and early stopping need follow-up.

perOption.r3:c1: Benzodiazepines with opioids raise overdose risk.
perOption.r3:c2: Benzodiazepines with opioids raise overdose risk.

exhibits.body: A 27-year-old client arrives for the fourth time in 2 months with sudden chest tightness, pounding heart, shaking, tingling hands and a fear of dying that peaked within 10 minutes. The client now avoids driving and supermarkets. The client drinks 5 energy drinks a day.

rows.label: Hands
cells: Tingling around the mouth and fingers

caseStudies.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder with exposure and response prevention

exhibits.title: Mental health unit
exhibits.body: A 33-year-old client with obsessive-compulsive disorder is admitted because handwashing now takes 5 hours a day. The client fears contaminating their baby and checks the stove 30 times before leaving. The client knows the fears are excessive. The client's hands are cracked and bleeding.

caseStudies.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder in a veteran

exhibits.title: Veterans clinic
exhibits.body: A 36-year-old veteran returned from combat 2 years ago. The veteran has nightmares most nights, startles at loud noises, avoids crowds and fireworks, and says, "I feel numb, like I'm watching my life on TV." The veteran drinks 8 beers most nights to sleep. The veteran's partner reports angry outbursts.

rows.label: Firearm at home
cells: Yes, loaded in the bedside drawer

rows.label: Suicidal thoughts
cells: "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off"

exhibits.title: Emergency department
exhibits.body: A 31-year-old client was found unresponsive in a restroom with a needle nearby. Paramedics gave naloxone 4 mg nasally twice. The client says the last use was "fentanyl, I think."

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
